Gen.1: God creates the heavens and the earth in six days, orders light, sky, land, and living things, and rests on the seventh day.
Gen.2: The creation account focuses on the garden, the man formed from dust, the command about the tree, and the woman made from his side.
Gen.3: The serpent questions God's word, the man and woman eat the forbidden fruit, and God pronounces judgment and clothes them.
Gen.4: Cain and Abel bring offerings, Cain murders his brother, and the line of Cain is set beside the birth of Seth.
Gen.5: A genealogy from Adam to Noah records the long lifespans and the refrain that each man died, with Enoch taken by God.
Gen.6: Human wickedness spreads, God resolves to judge the earth, and Noah is commanded to build an ark.
Gen.7: Noah, his family, and the animals enter the ark, the flood covers the earth, and the waters prevail for a hundred and fifty days.
Gen.8: God remembers Noah, the waters recede, the dove returns with an olive leaf, and Noah builds an altar.
Gen.9: God establishes his covenant with Noah and the rainbow sign, blesses his sons, and Noah curses Canaan.
Gen.10: The table of nations traces the descendants of Noah's sons and the founding of cities and peoples.
Gen.11: Humanity builds the tower of Babel, God scatters the languages, and the genealogy runs from Shem to Terah.
Gen.12: God calls Abram to leave his country with a promise of land, nation, and blessing, and Abram journeys to Canaan and Egypt.
Gen.13: Abram and Lot separate over pasture, Lot chooses the Jordan plain, and God renews the land promise to Abram.
Gen.14: A coalition of kings raids the plain, Abram rescues Lot, and Melchizedek blesses Abram, who refuses the spoils.
Gen.15: God cuts a covenant with Abram, promises descendants like the stars, and Abram believes and is counted righteous.
Gen.16: Sarai gives Hagar to Abram, Hagar conceives and despises her mistress, and the angel promises Ishmael.
Gen.17: God confirms the covenant, renames Abram and Sarai, institutes circumcision, and promises a son by Sarah.
Gen.18: Three visitors announce Isaac's birth, Sarah laughs, and Abraham intercedes for Sodom.
Gen.19: Two angels visit Lot in Sodom, the city is destroyed with fire, and Lot's wife looks back.
Gen.20: Abraham passes Sarah off as his sister to Abimelech, who is warned in a dream and restores her.
Gen.21: Isaac is born, Hagar and Ishmael are sent away, and Abraham makes a treaty at Beersheba.
Gen.22: God tests Abraham with the command to offer Isaac, the ram is provided, and the covenant promise is confirmed.
Gen.23: Sarah dies and Abraham buys the cave of Machpelah as a burial place.
Gen.24: Abraham's servant travels to find a wife for Isaac, Rebekah shows hospitality at the well, and she returns with him.
Gen.25: Abraham dies, Ishmael's line is recorded, and the twins Esau and Jacob are born to Isaac and Rebekah.
Gen.26: Isaac settles in Gerar, repeats the sister deception, digs wells, and makes a covenant with Abimelech.
Gen.27: Jacob deceives Isaac and takes Esau's blessing, and Esau vows to kill him.
Gen.28: Jacob flees, dreams of a ladder at Bethel, and God renews the covenant promise to him.
Gen.29: Jacob works for Laban, is deceived with Leah, and marries both Leah and Rachel.
Gen.30: Jacob's sons are born through Leah, Rachel, and their servants, and Jacob's flocks multiply through an agreement with Laban.
Gen.31: Jacob flees from Laban, Rachel steals the household gods, and the two make a covenant at Mizpah.
Gen.32: Jacob prepares to meet Esau, wrestles with a man until daybreak, and is renamed Israel.
Gen.33: Jacob and Esau meet and reconcile, and Jacob settles near Shechem.
Gen.34: Shechem violates Dinah, her brothers Simeon and Levi slaughter the men of the city, and Jacob fears the response.
Gen.35: Jacob returns to Bethel, Rachel dies giving birth to Benjamin, and Isaac dies.
Gen.36: The genealogy of Esau records the Edomite clans and kings.
Gen.37: Joseph receives dreams, is given a colorful coat, is thrown into a pit, and is sold into slavery in Egypt.
Gen.38: Judah leaves his brothers, marries, and is confronted by Tamar, who bears Perez and Zerah.
Gen.39: Joseph serves in Potiphar's house, is falsely accused by his wife, and is imprisoned.
Gen.40: Joseph interprets the dreams of Pharaoh's cupbearer and baker in prison.
Gen.41: Joseph interprets Pharaoh's dreams of famine, is raised to govern Egypt, and stores grain in the years of plenty.
Gen.42: Jacob sends his sons to Egypt for grain, Joseph recognizes them, and demands they bring Benjamin.
Gen.43: The brothers return with Benjamin, Joseph feasts with them, and his emotion shows.
Gen.44: Joseph tests the brothers with a silver cup, Judah offers himself in Benjamin's place.
Gen.45: Joseph reveals himself to his brothers, forgives them, and invites the family to Egypt.
Gen.46: Jacob travels to Egypt with his household and is reunited with Joseph in Goshen.
Gen.47: Joseph settles his family, administers the famine for Pharaoh, and Jacob blesses Pharaoh.
Gen.48: Jacob adopts Joseph's sons Ephraim and Manasseh and blesses the younger above the older.
Gen.49: Jacob gathers his sons and pronounces a prophetic blessing on each tribe, then dies.
Gen.50: Jacob is buried at Machpelah, Joseph reassures his brothers, and his final words and death close the book.
Exo.1: Israel multiplies in Egypt, a new Pharaoh fears them, and orders the Hebrew midwives to kill the boys.
Exo.2: Moses is born, hidden in a basket, raised in Pharaoh's house, kills an Egyptian, and flees to Midian where he marries Zipporah.
Exo.3: God speaks to Moses from the burning bush, reveals his name, and commissions him to bring Israel out of Egypt.
Exo.4: Moses objects and is given signs, Aaron becomes his spokesman, and Israel believes the report of deliverance.
Exo.5: Moses and Aaron confront Pharaoh, who increases the burden of brickmaking, and the people turn on Moses.
Exo.6: God reassures Moses with the covenant name, and the genealogy of Moses and Aaron is recorded.
Exo.7: Aaron's staff becomes a serpent, and the first plague turns the Nile to blood.
Exo.8: Frogs, gnats, and flies strike Egypt while Goshen is spared, and Pharaoh's heart hardens.
Exo.9: Livestock disease, boils, and hail fall on Egypt, with a warning to shelter and a partial confession from Pharaoh.
Exo.10: Locusts and darkness cover the land, Pharaoh bargains, and Moses is driven out.
Exo.11: God announces the death of the firstborn and instructs Israel to ask the Egyptians for silver and gold.
Exo.12: The Passover is instituted, the firstborn of Egypt are struck, and Israel leaves in haste.
Exo.13: The firstborn are consecrated to God, and Israel travels by the wilderness road guided by cloud and fire.
Exo.14: Pharaoh pursues, the sea is divided, Israel crosses on dry ground, and the Egyptian army is drowned.
Exo.15: Moses and Israel sing the song of deliverance, and the bitter waters of Marah are made sweet.
Exo.16: Manna and quail are given in the wilderness, with instructions about gathering and the Sabbath.
Exo.17: Water comes from the rock at Horeb, and Israel defeats Amalek while Moses' hands are held up.
Exo.18: Jethro visits Moses, advises him to delegate judgment to able men, and the leaders are appointed.
Exo.19: Israel camps at Sinai, God descends in fire, and the people are consecrated to hear the covenant.
Exo.20: God speaks the Ten Commandments and instructs Israel to build a simple altar.
Exo.21: Laws are given on servitude, personal injury, and restitution.
Exo.22: Laws cover theft, property damage, borrowing, and the treatment of the vulnerable and the foreigner.
Exo.23: Laws on justice, the Sabbath year, the three feasts, and the promise of an angel to lead Israel.
Exo.24: The covenant is ratified with blood, the elders eat before God, and Moses enters the cloud on the mountain.
Exo.25: Instructions begin for the ark, the table, and the lampstand with its oil.
Exo.26: The tabernacle curtains, frames, and inner veil are described.
Exo.27: The bronze altar, the courtyard, and the lamp oil are specified.
Exo.28: Garments are described for Aaron and the priests, including the ephod and the breastpiece.
Exo.29: The ordination of priests is set out with sacrifices and the daily offerings.
Exo.30: Instructions cover the incense altar, the census tax, the basin, anointing oil, and incense.
Exo.31: Bezalel and Oholiab are named as craftsmen, the Sabbath rest is restated, and Moses receives the tablets.
Exo.32: Israel makes the golden calf, God threatens to destroy them, Moses intercedes, and the tablets are broken.
Exo.33: God agrees to go with Israel, and Moses asks to see his glory.
Exo.34: God proclaims his name and character, renews the covenant, and Moses' face shines.
Exo.35: The people contribute materials, and the craftsmen are appointed for the work.
Exo.36: The work begins on the tabernacle curtains, frames, and the people give more than is needed.
Exo.37: The ark, the mercy seat, the table, the lampstand, and the incense altar are built.
Exo.38: The bronze altar, the basin, and the courtyard are made, and the metals are inventoried.
Exo.39: The priestly garments are completed and the finished pieces are brought to Moses, who blesses the people.
Exo.40: The tabernacle is erected, the glory fills it, and cloud and fire direct Israel's journeys.
Lev.1: Instructions are given for burnt offerings from the herd, the flock, and from birds.
Lev.2: Grain offerings are described, with and without leaven, and the portion for the priests.
Lev.3: Peace offerings from the herd and the flock are specified, and the fat is reserved for God.
Lev.4: Sin offerings are given for the anointed priest, the congregation, a leader, and a common person.
Lev.5: Guilt offerings cover specific sins, testimony withheld, uncleanness, and breach of trust.
Lev.6: The law of each offering is restated with the priests' share and the altar fire kept burning.
Lev.7: The guilt offering, the peace offering, the fat, the blood, and the priests' portion are regulated.
Lev.8: Aaron and his sons are consecrated, and the ordination sacrifices are carried out over seven days.
Lev.9: Aaron's first offerings are made, the glory appears, and fire consumes the sacrifice.
Lev.10: Nadab and Abihu offer unauthorized fire and die, and rules are given for priestly conduct.
Lev.11: Clean and unclean animals, fish, birds, and creeping things are distinguished.
Lev.12: Purification rules are given for women after childbirth.
Lev.13: The priest is instructed how to diagnose skin disease and inspect it week by week.
Lev.14: Cleansing rituals for skin disease and for mold in a house are described.
Lev.15: Bodily discharges and their cleansing are regulated.
Lev.16: The Day of Atonement is established with the scapegoat and the entry into the holy place.
Lev.17: Blood is forbidden as food, sacrifice is limited to the tabernacle, and the sanctity of blood is explained.
Lev.18: Sexual relations are restricted and the practices of Egypt and Canaan are forbidden.
Lev.19: Holiness commands cover respect for parents, the Sabbath, gleaning, honesty, and love of neighbor.
Lev.20: Penalties are given for idolatry, forbidden relations, and other capital offenses.
Lev.21: Rules govern how priests may contract uncleanness and whom they may marry.
Lev.22: Who may eat holy things and the requirement that offerings be without blemish are set out.
Lev.23: The appointed feasts are listed with their offerings and dates through the year.
Lev.24: The lampstand is maintained, the bread of the Presence is set out, and the case of the blasphemer sets a law of restitution.
Lev.25: The Sabbath year, the Year of Jubilee, and the redemption of land and slaves are established.
Lev.26: Blessings for obedience and curses for disobedience are set out, with a promise of restoration on confession.
Lev.27: Vows, dedications, and the redemption of persons and property are valued and regulated.
